sections.report:
I checked one section, "The whole piece", and one line fails: the main image is a placeholder, not a real photo. It takes up the biggest area on the page and says nothing about the event.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No.
   - **Where:** The picture at about x 48–648, y 92–422 is the largest and darkest thing on the screen, so it is where the eye lands first.
   - **What the viewer gets:** A generic grey head-and-shoulders silhouette, the kind used as a default avatar. Only the headline below says this is Ines Varga and her novel *The Salt Year*. The picture doesn't show the author, the book cover or the island the talk is about, so it adds nothing to the headline. It also tells the viewer the page isn't finished. For a bookshop event, a real face or cover is much of what makes someone come: they recognise the author, or the cover makes them curious.
   - **Why:** This is common sense and my own judgement. The catalogue's source for this rule (Bernbach/DDB) is not on the approved list, so I'm not citing it.
   - **Fix:** Use a real author portrait or the book cover. A cover set against an image of the island would tie in with the talk. If the silhouette is a fallback for an image that failed to load, that would explain it. In that case, check the live page and make the fallback something about the event, such as the cover or the title set as type, not an anonymous person.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.

**What's working.**
- **The copy reads clearly to a stranger.** The date and time ("Thursday 13 November, 7 pm") come first and stand out in warm brown. The headline names the author, says this is a new novel and gives its title. The supporting line says exactly what happens: a reading, a talk about the island, then questions, with drinks from 6.30 pm. A viewer doesn't have to guess at anything they would act on.
- **The call to action is specific.** "Book a free seat" names exactly what the button does and removes the cost worry in the same two words. That is much stronger than "Register" or "Learn more". There is one button on the page and it is styled clearly.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the silhouette is the intended image or one that failed to load. Check it in a live browser.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea together), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- There is a clear order. The dark photo block (48–648 × 92–422 px) is the largest and darkest shape on the page, so the eye lands there first. It then drops to the headline at about 34 px bold (y ≈ 472–548), which is roughly twice the size of anything else in the text. After that the eye moves to the body text and the button. That order fits an event page. Keep the headline as the only large text. One caution for the director: the photo leads the page, but it is a grey placeholder silhouette, so the eye starts on an empty spot. That belongs to the pictures section, not here.
- The text levels are easy to tell apart. The date, at about 14 px, is bold and rust-coloured. The headline, at about 34 px, is bold and near-black. The body, at about 17 px, is regular weight and softer grey. The button text is bold and white on a dark fill. The small sizes sit close together (date about 14, nav and button about 15, body about 17), but each one also differs in weight, colour or placement, so they don't read as mistakes. The headline differs from the body in weight and colour as well as size.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content (picture, date, headline, body and button) sits in one column from x=48 to 648. The darkest, heaviest thing on the page, the 600×330 photo block (x 48–648, y 92–422), is in the top-left corner. To its right, a field about 584 px wide (x 648–1232, y 92–672) holds nothing. The only things at right are the four small grey nav links. The viewer sees a page that tips left and looks unfinished, as if a second column (a sidebar, more events, booking details) failed to load or was never designed. The space is gathered, but nothing in it sets up the tension Ruder describes between open and dense areas. It reads as left over, not chosen, so it also gives no reason to stay on the page. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") holds that a heavy side needs a counterweight. Direction of the fix: give the right side something that earns its weight. Here that is most naturally the practical facts a reader acts on (date, time, place, price "free", seats left, the Book button), or the book cover. Or, if this event really stands alone, make the layout own it: let the picture run wider across the page, or centre the column so the empty space reads as framing. **Defect, major.** It is the main reason the page looks unfinished, and the facts that would fill the space are the ones that move a reader to book.

**What's working.**
- One clean left edge. The picture, date, headline, body and button all start at exactly x=48, the same edge as the logo, so the column reads as one unit with no near-misses.
- The spacing shows the groups. There is about 32 px from the picture to the date, then tighter steps from date to headline (about 16) and headline to body (about 10), and about 20 to the button. The date, title, description and ask read as one event block, with the date sitting on the headline it introduces.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (the visual weight balances).

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes, Text).** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied, so I judged from the whole 1280×800 image.
1 body size yes · 2 captions/labels yes · 3 plain face yes · 4 one family yes · 5 small-text weight yes · 6 contrast yes · 7 text over image yes (none) · 8 measure yes (first line ~77 chars, a two-line blurb, borderline but fine) · 9 leading yes · 10 heading leading yes · 11 flush left yes · 12 justified yes (none) · 13 rag yes · 14 widows yes · 15 heading breaks at phrase boundaries **no** ("…on her / new novel") · 16 paragraph marks yes · 17 left edge yes · 18 chunking yes · 19 mixed case yes · 20 emphasis yes · 21 display tracking yes · 22 kerning yes · 23 tracking yes · 24 caps spacing yes (none) · 25 ligatures yes (no fi/fl) · 26 real cuts yes · 27 quotes/dashes yes (none needed) · 28 tabular figures yes (none) · 29 real type yes · 30 nothing clipped yes.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The headline at about x 48–612, y 472–548 breaks as "An evening with Ines Varga on her / new novel, The Salt Year". The break splits "her new novel" in the middle, so line one ends on a dangling "on her" and the reader has to carry the half-phrase over to line two. The headline has two parts: who (Ines Varga) and what (her new novel, *The Salt Year*). A break after "Varga" would put one part on each line: "An evening with Ines Varga / on her new novel, The Salt Year". The direction of the fix is a manual break, or a `text-wrap: balance` setting checked by eye, so each line holds one complete phrase. You'd also need to check where it breaks at narrower widths. This is a convention (and my common-sense judgement: I couldn't open the catalog entry because Bash was denied). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **Clear type scale with few steps.** I count four levels: a ~36 px bold headline, ~17 px body, a ~14 px bold date label and ~14 px nav. The step from headline to everything else is big. The date is set apart by colour and weight rather than an extra size, so each size has an obvious job.
- **The date and time read first and clearly.** "Thursday 13 November, 7 pm" sits in bold rust above the headline, with comfortable contrast on white. The detail a visitor acts on is easy to find and hard to misread.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**First read.** The eye goes to the dark picture block (48–648 × 92–422), then down to the near-black headline, then to the black "Book a free seat" button. This is a bookshop's event page for an author reading. It feels calm, warm and plain. The picture is a placeholder silhouette, not a photo.

**Job (assumed).** An event page that gets local readers to book a free seat at the reading.

**Walk: Color**
- Small palette: yes. It uses a warm near-black, white, mid-gray for the nav and body text, and one warm brown for the date.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. The only hue is the brown date line, about 200 px wide. The rest is neutral.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. The dark picture, the near-black headline and button, and the white page still show the structure in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. The warm brown is on the date, which is the key fact. The cooler grays are on the nav, which sits back.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The headline, button fill and logo look like the same near-black.
- No vibrating edges: yes. There are no neighboring saturated colors.
- Status colors: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. The brown date is also set apart by its position and weight. No nav item is marked by color.
- Dark theme gray, not black: yes. The page is light, and the picture block is a warm dark gray, not pure black.

No line was answered no or unsure, so step 5 opens no entries.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One warm accent on the one fact that matters.** The date ("Thursday 13 November, 7 pm", around 48,455) is the only hued text on the page. The brown makes the when stand out without a badge or a box. Because it is the only hue, it stays the clear signal; a second accent would weaken it. The brown looks dark enough for the 4.5:1 contrast that WCAG 1.4.3 asks of normal text, but that is by eye; measure it to confirm.
- **The neutrals are warm and consistent.** The picture block, the headline and the button all lean to the same warm brown-black, so the page reads as one considered palette that suits a bookshop, not default cool grays. The button is the darkest solid fill below the picture, so its dark value marks it as the place to act.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The picture is a gray silhouette placeholder. If a real author photo replaces it, the photo's colors and how dark it is will change how strongly that block pulls the eye ahead of the headline. Check it with the real image.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one picture, the event image, plus the "Margin Books" wordmark.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. The only picture on the page (x48–648, y92–422, about 600×330 px and the largest element on screen) is a generic grey head-and-shoulders silhouette on a dark gradient. It's a default avatar placeholder. It doesn't show Ines Varga or the cover of *The Salt Year*.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The eye goes to this block first, so the first thing a visitor sees is an image with no information in it. It reads as "photo missing" or an unfinished page, which costs the shop credibility. It also wastes the one spot that could make someone want to come: the author's face, the book cover, or the room where the reading happens.
   - **Why:** There's no catalog entry for this line, so it's common sense. A placeholder in the hero slot is the most-viewed failure on the page.
   - **Fix:** Put in a real photo of the author or the book's cover art. If the image failed to load or was a deliberate stand-in during the build, the finding goes away once a real image is in place, so check the live page. If no image exists, drop the block and let the date and headline lead rather than show a stand-in.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect, major.

**What's working.**
- The "Margin Books" wordmark (top left, about x48–175, y18–38) is a plain bold text mark with generous clear space and no distortion. It stays readable at any size and in one colour.
- The picture frame itself is well set. Its left edge lines up with the text column at x48, and its corners are slightly rounded to match the button. A real photo dropped into this slot would sit cleanly in the layout.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the silhouette is the intended design or a fallback after the real image failed to load. Check the live page and the image source.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content)

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image has no chart, table of figures or dashboard. It is a bookshop event page with a hero image, a date, a headline, body copy and one button.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a header navigation (Events, New in, Gift cards, Find us) and one call-to-action button, "Book a free seat". The crop script was refused, so I worked from the whole image. At about 1280×800 it is one screen, so it would not have been cut into crops anyway.

**Findings**
1. *Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them instead of making them hunt for it?* No. The booking block runs from about x 48–648, y 444–672. It gives the date, the time and what happens, then goes straight to "Book a free seat" (about x 48–210, y 625–672). Nothing next to the button says where the evening takes place, how many seats are left, or what booking involves: an account, a name only, or something else. Someone about to commit to an evening needs the place first. To find it they must leave for "Find us", or tap the button without knowing what comes next. Tognazzini's Anticipation principle is off the approved list, so this is common sense. Fix: put the venue on the date line or right above the button, such as "Margin Books, <street>", plus a short line under the button about what booking takes ("Takes 30 seconds, no account needed") or how many seats are left, if that is true. Defect. Weight: minor, though it moves toward major if the shop has more than one branch.
2. *Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step?* No. In the header nav (about x 952–1232, y 22–40), "Events" looks the same as "New in", "Gift cards" and "Find us": same grey, same weight, no underline or background. The visitor is on an event page, but the menu doesn't say which part of the site they are in. They can't tell this event is one of a list, or that "Events" leads to the others. Laubheimer, "Menu-Design Checklist" (Nielsen Norman Group), guideline 5, under Nielsen heuristic 1. Fix (approved): mark the current page in the navigation menu with one clear cue, such as a bolder weight, an underline, or a background, so that the person can see where they are. Convention. Weight: minor.
3. *Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?* No. "New in" suggests the site sells books, but the header has no search field or search icon. Looking up a title is a bookshop site's most frequent action, so anyone who arrives here from an event link and wants a book has to browse instead. Nielsen heuristic 7, "Flexibility and efficiency of use". Fix: add a search entry point to the header, at the right end of the nav, where people expect it. Convention. Weight: minor for this event page, more on the site as a whole.

**What's working.** There is exactly one action on the page. "Book a free seat" is the only filled control, and its near-black fill stands well apart from the grey text-only nav, so the primary action is clear at a glance. The label names one exact act and its cost ("free"), so the visitor knows what they're agreeing to before they press it. The button also looks plenty big for a target (about 162×47 px), and the nav words have about 26 px between them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the button and nav links show a focus indicator at least 2 px thick at 3:1 contrast, and whether they have hover and pressed states. This matters because the whole page funnels to one button. Also what "Book a free seat" opens, and whether that next step has a way out.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (shows where the user is; shortcuts for frequent actions; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 2 unsure (focus indicator visible; focus not obscured)
